title: User Account Changes
exclusions: Covers local Linux user and group management records emitted to the Linux Audit subsystem and writes to the four configured local identity databases. It does not cover accounts held only in Active Directory, LDAP, FreeIPA, an identity provider, a container image, or an offline filesystem; prove which account changed during an unstructured direct file write; recover events lost before forwarding; detect disabled or tampered auditing; or establish that a change was unauthorized, malicious, or compliant. Authentication logs are not used as a substitute for account-management audit records.
evidence: When deployed, retain the managed identity-file audit rules, effective `auditctl -l` output, the `linux_user_account_changes` saved-search definition and ACL, scheduler and triggered-alert history, and exported result rows containing `firstTime`, `host`, `audit_event_id`, `action`, `object_category`, `target`, `actor`, `effective_user`, `operation`, `result`, `executable`, and `record_types`. These artefacts demonstrate operation of the collection and search during the retained intervals; they do not prove continuous host coverage or authorization of each change.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Into an isolated `index=os` test input with `sourcetype=auditd`, index `type=ADD_USER msg=audit(1761643200.100:811): pid=2401 uid=0 auid=1001 ses=4 msg='op=adding-user acct="uc118_test" exe="/usr/sbin/useradd" hostname=? addr=? terminal=pts/3 res=success' UID="root" AUID="tester"`. The search must return exactly one row with `audit_event_id=1761643200.100:811`, `action=created`, `object_category=user`, `target=uc118_test`, `actor=tester`, `result=success`, and `executable=/usr/sbin/useradd`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Into a separate isolated interval, index a `type=USER_LOGIN` record for `acct="uc118_test"` and a `type=SYSCALL` record with `key=software_update`; keep the other fields similar to the positive record. The search must return zero rows because a login is not an account change and the syscall was not selected by the `identity` audit key.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=auditd` events produced by the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux `rlog.sh` scripted input, which reads `/var/log/audit/audit.log` and translates records with `ausearch`. The semantic branch requires `type` values `ADD_USER`, `DEL_USER`, `USER_MGMT`, `USER_CHAUTHTOK`, `ACCT_LOCK`, `ACCT_UNLOCK`, `ADD_GROUP`, `DEL_GROUP`, `GRP_MGMT`, or `GRP_CHAUTHTOK`; context uses `msg`, `pid`, `uid`/`UID`, `auid`/`AUID`, `op`, `acct`, `grp`, `id`/`ID`, `exe`, `terminal`, and `res`. The direct-write fallback requires persistent `identity` watches on `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/group`, and `/etc/gshadow`, producing `SYSCALL` and `PATH` records with `key`, `success`, and `name`. `os` is a local index convention.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) 10.2.0 or a later version whose `rlog.sh` and `auditd` source contract has been regression-tested locally. No premium Splunk app is required.

splunkbaseApps.name: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux

spl:
index=os sourcetype=auditd (type IN (ADD_USER,DEL_USER,USER_MGMT,USER_CHAUTHTOK,ACCT_LOCK,ACCT_UNLOCK,ADD_GROUP,DEL_GROUP,GRP_MGMT,GRP_CHAUTHTOK) OR (type=SYSCALL key=identity) OR (type=PATH name IN ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","/etc/group","/etc/gshadow")))
| rex field=_raw "msg=audit\((?<audit_event_id>[^\)]+)\)"
| where isnotnull(audit_event_id)
| eval audit_type=upper(type), actor_record=coalesce(AUID,auid), effective_user_record=coalesce(UID,uid), operation_record=op, target_record=coalesce(acct,grp,ID,id), executable_record=exe, result_record=lower(coalesce(res,success)), account_event=if(in(audit_type,"ADD_USER","DEL_USER","USER_MGMT","USER_CHAUTHTOK","ACCT_LOCK","ACCT_UNLOCK","ADD_GROUP","DEL_GROUP","GRP_MGMT","GRP_CHAUTHTOK"),audit_type,null()), identity_watch=if(key="identity","identity",null()), identity_path=if(audit_type="PATH",name,null())
| stats earliest(_time) as firstTime latest(_time) as lastTime values(audit_type) as record_types values(account_event) as account_event_types values(identity_watch) as identity_watch values(identity_path) as identity_paths values(actor_record) as actors values(effective_user_record) as effective_users values(operation_record) as operations values(target_record) as targets values(executable_record) as executables values(result_record) as results values(pid) as pids by host audit_event_id
| where isnotnull(account_event_types) OR isnotnull(identity_watch)
| eval action=case(mvfind(account_event_types,"^(ADD_USER|ADD_GROUP)$")>=0,"created",mvfind(account_event_types,"^(DEL_USER|DEL_GROUP)$")>=0,"deleted",mvfind(account_event_types,"^ACCT_LOCK$")>=0,"locked",mvfind(account_event_types,"^ACCT_UNLOCK$")>=0,"unlocked",isnotnull(account_event_types),"modified",true(),"identity_database_write"), object_category=case(mvfind(account_event_types,"(GROUP|GRP)")>=0,"group",isnotnull(account_event_types),"user",true(),"account_database"), target=coalesce(mvindex(targets,0),mvjoin(identity_paths,","),"unknown"), actor=coalesce(mvindex(actors,0),"unknown"), effective_user=coalesce(mvindex(effective_users,0),"unknown"), operation=coalesce(mvindex(operations,0),"not_reported"), result=coalesce(mvindex(results,0),"unknown"), executable=coalesce(mvindex(executables,0),"unknown"), pid=coalesce(mvindex(pids,0),"unknown")
| table firstTime lastTime host audit_event_id action object_category target actor effective_user operation result executable pid record_types identity_paths
| sort 0 -firstTime
description: Reports one row per Linux Audit event when a local user or group is created, deleted, locked, unlocked, or modified, or when a configured audit watch records a write attempt against a local identity database. It preserves the reported actor, target, operation, outcome, executable, and Audit event identifier without treating command-name text in an authentication log as proof of a change.
value: Detecting unexpected account, credential, lock-state, group, and identity-file changes helps prevent persistent unauthorized access and disruption of legitimate administration. Outcome-aware records improve comparison of the exact host, actor, process, and target with approved lifecycle work while retaining failed attempts and collection limitations.
implementation: Enable Linux Audit and the add-on's `rlog.sh` input, verify semantic account-management records from the host's supported user-management tools, and add persistent write/attribute watches for the four local identity databases to cover direct edits. Route the translated output to `index=os sourcetype=auditd`, validate field extraction with controlled fixtures, then run the search every five minutes over a ten-minute lookback and alert on each returned Audit event.
visualization: Use a newest-first table showing time, host, action, object category, target, actor, operation, result, executable, and Audit event ID. Add timecharts by action and result, a panel for direct identity-database writes, and breakdowns by actor and host role. Drill down to all records sharing `host,audit_event_id`; display unknown targets as telemetry gaps rather than inferred account names.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the primary `sourcetype=auditd` search. Splunk documents the add-on's translated `auditd` input as having no CIM data-model mapping. Do not use an accelerated Change search unless a separate, tested normalization maps these records to the Change.Account_Management dataset.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **`systemd-sysusers` during RPM or DEB installation** — Packages legitimately create service users and groups. Confirm `executable`, account name or numeric ID, package-manager transaction, package signature, and the matching `sysusers.d` declaration. Suppress notification only for an exact package, host role, expected account, and bounded deployment window in `linux_account_change_exceptions.csv`; retain the row in the audit dashboard.

2. **Ansible, Puppet, Chef, or Salt account convergence** — A managed user, password hash, shell, or group membership can be corrected on many hosts. Match `actor`, executable, automation job ID, inventory scope, and approved change record. Use a time-bound exception keyed by automation identity, host role, action, target, `valid_from`, `valid_until`, `change_id`, and owner; do not allow-list all activity by root.

3. **Cloud-init first-boot provisioning** — Image launch can create the declared administrator and service accounts. Verify the instance creation time, cloud-init run identifier, signed image version, and account declaration in the launch configuration. Limit suppression to the named image and account during the documented bootstrap interval; account changes after bootstrap remain alertable.

4. **CyberArk, Delinea, BeyondTrust, or another approved password-rotation job** — Rotation can produce `USER_CHAUTHTOK` or related `USER_MGMT` events. Correlate the target with a successful vault job and the expected service-account schedule. Suppress only the matching vault service identity, target account, host scope, and short rotation window; failed results and unexpected executables remain visible.

5. **HR offboarding or emergency access revocation** — IAM operations may delete or lock an account and remove group memberships. Confirm the employee or contractor case, approving operator, target host scope, and execution timestamp. Notification can be routed as informational for an exact case-bound exception, but deletion and lock evidence must not be discarded.

6. **Approved editing or replacement of `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/group`, or `/etc/gshadow`** — `vipw`, `vigr`, a configuration agent, package script, or recovery procedure can trigger the identity watch even when the resulting semantic change is expected. Compare all records sharing the Audit event ID, inspect `exe`, and verify the resulting file through approved integrity tooling. Never suppress arbitrary writes by path alone; key the exception to executable, actor, host, ticket, and expiry.
reviewer: documentation review against Linux Audit, Red Hat, Splunk, and MITRE ATT&CK sources; no runtime or SME sign-off
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and scope

Use a supported Linux distribution with the kernel Audit subsystem enabled and `auditd` operating normally. Install the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) on the Universal Forwarder and make its search-time knowledge available on the search tier. Splunk Security Content identifies add-on 10.2.0 for its current Linux Auditd Add User data source; this editorial review did not execute the input or SPL on a live Splunk release, so confirm the current compatibility matrix and regression-test the installed version before production use. Create or select the operating-system index and grant the detection role read access. This catalogue uses `index=os`; change that term consistently if the deployment uses another name.

The Linux Audit project defines dedicated records for account manipulation. `ADD_USER` and `DEL_USER` identify additions and deletions; `USER_MGMT`, `USER_CHAUTHTOK`, `ACCT_LOCK`, and `ACCT_UNLOCK` cover attribute, credential, and lock-state operations. The corresponding group types are included because group creation, deletion, credential changes, and membership-related administration can change effective access. These are user-space Audit messages from participating account-management software, not strings inferred from `/var/log/secure` or `/var/log/auth.log`. A bespoke tool that edits an identity file without emitting libaudit account messages creates a blind spot, so the implementation also watches the local account databases. Neither source proves malicious intent.

## Step 1 — Configure data collection and verify Linux Audit coverage

Under configuration management, create a persistent rules file such as `/etc/audit/rules.d/40-local-identity.rules` with the following file watches:

```text
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/group -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/gshadow -p wa -k identity
```

The `w` and `a` permissions record writes and attribute changes. These watches complement, rather than generate, the semantic account records. Load them through the distribution-supported workflow, commonly `augenrules --load`, and inspect `auditctl -l`. If the ruleset is immutable, use the controlled reboot procedure instead of disabling immutability. Hosts that use other local account databases need separately reviewed rules; do not assume these four paths represent LDAP, FreeIPA, or accounts baked into images.

Verify the native records on a disposable host with approved test accounts. Run a bounded `ausearch -m ADD_USER,DEL_USER,USER_MGMT,USER_CHAUTHTOK,ACCT_LOCK,ACCT_UNLOCK,ADD_GROUP,DEL_GROUP,GRP_MGMT,GRP_CHAUTHTOK -i` and inspect `type`, event timestamp and serial, `pid`, login user, effective user, `op`, account or ID, `exe`, terminal, and `res`. Field presence and operation wording vary by distribution and shadow-utils build. Record that variation; never invent a target name when only a numeric or unknown ID is reported. Separately monitor audit backlog, disk actions, and lost-record counters because a quiet search cannot distinguish no changes from broken auditing.

### Configure Splunk collection and parsing

Enable the add-on-supplied `rlog.sh` stanza in a local configuration layer, not by editing the add-on's defaults. The effective stanza should retain `sourcetype=auditd`, route to the selected index, and use the supported interval. `rlog.sh` reads `/var/log/audit/audit.log` and translates records with `ausearch`; the forwarder service account therefore needs the privileges documented for the installed add-on and distribution. Do not run the whole forwarder as root merely to bypass a failed permission design. Apply a reviewed group, ACL, or service capability model, then test it after forwarder upgrades.

Use `splunk btool inputs list --debug` on the forwarder to identify the winning stanza and confirm `disabled`, `index`, `source`, `sourcetype`, and interval. Search `index=os sourcetype=auditd earliest=-15m` and compare a bounded interval with `ausearch` on the same host. Verify that one Audit record is not duplicated by a second file monitor and that `msg=audit(...:serial)` survives in `_raw`. Confirm extraction of `type`, `pid`, `auid`/`AUID`, `uid`/`UID`, `op`, target account or ID, `exe`, and `res`; for watch events confirm `key=identity`, `success`, and associated `PATH name` records.

Do not substitute `linux_secure`: authentication logs may show a program invocation or PAM activity but do not provide the dedicated account-change record contract. Also do not silently substitute `linux_audit`. Splunk's source-type table maps `linux_audit` to Authentication and Change but maps the translated `auditd` source used here to no CIM model. The primary SPL intentionally has no `cimSpl`; a local Change.Account_Management mapping is a separate engineering artefact that must normalize actor versus target, action, result, object category, and event identity before acceleration.

## Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_user_account_changes`. The base search admits the ten documented semantic account/group types. Its second branch admits the SYSCALL record carrying `key=identity`; its third admits PATH records for the four watched files. `rex` extracts the Audit timestamp-and-serial value from raw text. `stats` groups records only by `host,audit_event_id`, joining a watch's SYSCALL and PATH context without the memory and ordering costs of `transaction`. Rows without a parseable Audit identifier are deliberately excluded and must be surfaced by a separate data-quality search, not merged under a guessed identity.

The normalization assigns `created`, `deleted`, `locked`, `unlocked`, or `modified` only from a semantic record type. A watch-only event is labelled `identity_database_write`, not a particular user change, because a file write does not identify the affected account by itself. `res` is used for user-space messages and `success` for syscall records. Both successful and failed operations remain visible. A failed result is an attempt or tool failure, not a completed account change.

Schedule every five minutes with earliest `-10m@m` and latest `@m` to tolerate modest forwarding delay. Trigger when result count is greater than zero. If per-result notifications are enabled, throttle for ten minutes on `host,audit_event_id`; never throttle only by host or actor because that can hide a second change. Preserve every result in the dashboard or summary destination even when routing is suppressed. Start with all changes reviewable, then route successful creation, credential, lock, and privileged-group operations according to local severity policy. No universal numeric threshold is appropriate for discrete account lifecycle events.

## Step 3 — Validate the control and parsing

Run the positive and negative `controlTest` scenarios against an isolated test index first. The positive ADD_USER record must produce one `created` user row with the exact event ID, target, actor, result, and executable. The USER_LOGIN and unrelated-key SYSCALL records must produce no rows. Add a failed `USER_CHAUTHTOK` record and confirm it remains visible with `action=modified` and `result=failed`; do not relabel it as a successful password change.

Next index a paired test event with the same Audit identifier: one `type=SYSCALL key=identity success=yes` record and one `type=PATH name="/etc/passwd"` record. Expect one `identity_database_write` row whose `identity_paths` contains `/etc/passwd`. Change the key to `software_update` and confirm that the same path record alone is removed after aggregation. This verifies both the positive watch branch and its guard against unrelated PATH context.

On a disposable Linux host, use an approved lifecycle test to create, modify, lock, unlock, and delete a non-privileged test account. Compare in the Splunk Search interface each indexed semantic row against `ausearch -i` output by serial number. Perform a separately approved `vipw` test to confirm the identity watch. Record missing fields as parser findings. Finally, run `index=os sourcetype=auditd | timechart span=5m count by host limit=0` over a representative period and investigate silent hosts, but remember that event-driven Audit data can legitimately be sparse; corroborate collection health with forwarder and auditd telemetry.

## Step 4 — Operationalize and troubleshoot

Build a restricted table with the fields emitted by the SPL, a trend by action and result, a watch-only panel, and drilldowns to all raw records sharing the host and Audit event ID. Restrict broad access because account names, terminals, source addresses, and command context can be sensitive. The runbook should identify the host owner, determine whether the actor and executable are expected, compare the target and operation with the lifecycle or change record, inspect related package and automation activity, and verify the current account or group state using approved administration tools. Do not automatically reverse a deletion, password change, or identity-file write from the alert alone.

MITRE ATT&CK T1136.001 applies when a local account is created for persistence; T1098 applies when an existing account or its permissions are manipulated to preserve or elevate access. The broad audit search also returns ordinary administration, failed attempts, deletions, and group maintenance that do not instantiate either technique. Apply the ATT&CK labels only after the record type and investigative context support them.

Preserve the managed rule file, effective rules, input configuration, add-on version, saved-search definition, scheduler history, source events, result rows, alert disposition, and approved exceptions under the organization's retention and access policy. Record collection outages and dropped Audit events explicitly. These artefacts support operational review; they are not, by themselves, proof of complete auditing or regulatory compliance.

### Troubleshoot specific failure modes

* **No `auditd` events** — Confirm `auditd` is active, the audit log exists, the forwarder identity can execute the supported input and read required files, and `btool` shows the stanza enabled. Repair permissions through the approved least-privilege model.
* **Semantic records absent but watch events present** — The local account tool may lack audit integration or use a different record type. Compare with `ausearch -m ALL`; retain the watch fallback and document or normalize only observed types after review.
* **Account target is `unknown(UID)` or numeric** — The account may not yet resolve when `ausearch -i` translates it. Keep the reported ID, correlate with other records and the resulting database, and do not fabricate a username.
* **Watch writes lack a PATH row** — Search all raw records with the same host and Audit serial, verify event breaking, and check whether the PATH record arrived under the expected sourcetype. Fix collection before inferring a file.
* **Duplicate rows** — Look for overlapping `rlog.sh` and direct file monitors, duplicate deployment apps, or repeated ingestion after a seek-state problem. Deduplicate the input path; do not hide persistent duplication with `dedup host`.
* **`identity` rules disappear after reboot** — Confirm the rules file is in the distribution's persistent directory, inspect `augenrules --check` and load errors, and resolve ordering or immutable-rules behavior through configuration management.
* **Every actor appears as root** — Use login UID (`auid`/`AUID`) for the originating session and UID for the effective identity. If login UID is unset for a daemon, correlate with the automation service; do not assign the action to a human.
* **CIM tstats returns nothing while raw search works** — This is expected for `sourcetype=auditd` without a custom mapping. Do not enable acceleration as a workaround; build and validate the Change.Account_Management normalization first.
grandmaExplanation: We watch when local users or groups are added, removed, locked, unlocked, or changed on a Linux computer. That helps the team check whether the change was expected and spot attempts to create or alter access.
